title: NAB cultivates cheap talent offshore as Australian jobs are axed
full_text:
More than a third of National Australia Bank’s Vietnamese workforce is made up of interns and graduates fresh out of university who the bank mentors with hands-on technical training and coaching, for minimal cost.
NAB has come under fire this past week for axing 2500 workers as it looks to cut costs at a time when loan demand is slowing.
Equally, the big four bank is expanding its offshore workforce, with plans to add at least 180 new positions in India and Vietnam in the coming months, and potentially many more.
Insiders say NAB’s end game is to embrace artificial intelligence and that offshoring is a step on this path. By next year, the bank will have slashed 6 per cent of its 42,000-strong workforce as it looks to tighten its belt and ride out a subdued credit cycle.
When it’s time to dump technology workers in India and Vietnam in coming years, as AI advances, the bank will cull swathes of these offshore workers while being able to claim no Australian staff member will be made redundant as a result of AI, sources said.
Across the two countries, NAB now employs more than 7000 local workers, most of whom have been assembled over the past five years. Since 2021, NAB has run a tech internship, NAB StarCamp, at its “innovation centre” in Vietnam every three months.
The latest group of interns who made the cut, “Batch 24”, are just about to start the 12-week course. Once the traineeship is up, the vast majority – upwards of 90 per cent – will go on to be employed by the lender. StarCamp is a rolling program in Vietnam, with intakes every 12 weeks to ensure a continuous conveyor belt of talent comes into the bank. The numbers in each intake vary, but some have been as high as 70 graduates in a single 12-week block, The Australian understands.
All up, about 700 Vietnamese graduates have gone through the program, which pays each intern the equivalent of $600 a month. Almost all were handed jobs after their tech training course.
The cost savings for NAB are immediate. A junior software engineer in Vietnam might cost the bank about $20,000 a year, compared to $80,000 or more to hire an equivalent Australian worker.
NAB runs a similar StarCamp program in Melbourne but on a much smaller scale. Last year, it took in 40 interns. The Australian understands the next 10-week program, due to begin next month, will host 10-20 graduates.
The bank also runs other graduate programs in Melbourne but numbers appear to have dropped off substantially as the focus shifts to keeping frontline jobs in Australia and gradually offshoring tech competency.
In the wake of NAB announcing it would axe 2500 roles last Tuesday, staff are waiting to hear their fate. They will have to fight their colleagues for a limited number of roles as part of the restructure, with 1500 jobs destined to be eliminated by mid-December.
Bank sources said they did not expect roles in India and Vietnam to be affected by the cuts, which are widespread across the Australian operation including strategy, IT, transformation, compliance and risk, and people and culture departments. Branch roles are expected to be spared. On the day of the announcement, which sent NAB’s shares tumbling, NAB Vietnam posted new job ads, including for senior engineers.
The Financial Sector Union said it was appalled by NAB’s move to cut thousands of jobs, including 1500 before Christmas.
The union has already lodged a dispute with the lender over the job cuts, giving the bank until Monday to respond. “The actions of NAB management are despicable and have been compounded by the contemptuous way they have kept their workers in the dark,” FSU national assistant secretary Nicole McPherson said.
“NAB’s public statement was nothing but corporate spin but its intention is clear – NAB sees its workers as a barrier to profits and a problem that can be swept aside with ruthless cuts.” NAB shares closed on Friday at $41.31. On Tuesday, chief executive Andrew Irvine flagged $300m in pre-tax redundancy costs in 2026-27 from the restructure.
